title: Max Roach - Wikipedia
notes: Maxwell Lemuel Roach, born 10 January 1924, Newland Township, Pasquotank County, North Carolina; died 16 August 2007, New York City. Brooklyn from four; gospel bands at ten; subbed for Sonny Greer with Ellington in 1942; Manhattan School of Music (1950-53). One of the first bebop drummers with Kenny Clarke: 'playing the beat-by-beat pulse of standard 4/4 time on the ride cymbal instead of on the thudding bass drum'. Parker's Savoy sessions (1945), Debut Records with Mingus (1952), the quintet with Clifford Brown (1954-56), Jazz in 3/4 Time (1957), We Insist! (1960), Money Jungle (1962), Drums Unlimited (1966), M'Boom (1970s). 'The Drum Also Waltzes' was 'often quoted by John Bonham in his Moby Dick drum solo'. Traditional grip early, matched later. Influenced Joe Morello, Tony Williams, Jack DeJohnette, Peter Erskine, Billy Cobham, Ginger Baker, Mitch Mitchell. MacArthur fellowship 1988; DownBeat Hall of Fame 1980; Modern Drummer Hall of Fame 1992.

title: Remembering Max Roach, Rhythmic Innovator (NPR, 16 August 2007)
notes: 'one of the most accomplished and influential drummers of the 20th century, a master of polyrhythms and unpredictable beats'; helped father bebop; 'elevated the drums from background instrument to lead'. A press phrase: names no record and no device, so it is not a source for one.

title: Max Roach, 1924-2007 (Modern Drummer, October 2007: Ken Micallef, with tributes)
notes: Micallef: with Kenny Clarke he 'moved the jazz drummer's pulse ... to the ride cymbal and the hi-hat'; 'dropping explosive percussive "bombs" and exploring four-way coordination'. Richie Morales: 'a master of theme and variation, using motific and sequential ideas'; as a leader he 'used polyrhythms and odd time signatures in his arrangements'; hear Clifford Brown And Max Roach and Jazz In 3/4 Time. Bill Bruford played The Drum Also Waltzes as his homage.

title: Max Roach - Percussive Arts Society Hall of Fame
notes: Piano at eight, drums at ten. 'Jo Jones was the first drummer I heard who played broken rhythms'; admired Chick Webb's soloing, Sonny Greer, Cozy Cole and Sid Catlett, who 'incorporated this hi-hat and ride cymbal style'; Kenny Clarke. The ride cymbal as the centre of the kit; very fast tempos; solo drum compositions; tom-tom patterns from Caribbean and Cuban percussion. Parker quintet 1947-49, Birth of the Cool (1949), Jazz at Massey Hall (1953).

title: Steve Smith on the art and history of drum soloing (DRUM! Magazine)
notes: The Drum Also Waltzes: 'Max plays an ostinato with his feet - with the bass drum on 1 and the hi-hat on 2'; 'It has an ostinato, much like what Bozzio is doing now, but simplified'; 'a really nice one to use to work on the idea of soloing over an ostinato'; 'Max leaves space and plays beautiful phrasing'. Live 'the tempos are different, the melody/motif he plays changes'.

title: 11 Steps to 'The Drum Also Waltzes' Independence (BANG! The Drum School), parts 1 and 3
notes: 'the bass drum plays on beat one and the hi-hat plays on beat two. The feet rest on beat three and that repeats over and over again', while Roach solos with his hands; Neil Peart's version puts the hat on 2 and 3. Part 3: 'a drum solo based on a 3/4 foot ostinato.'

title: Antoine Chambert-Loir, Max Roach's 100 (listening notes, 2024)
notes: The Drum Also Waltzes: 'a waltz groove sustained by Roach's hi-hat that plays regularly on the second beat of each 3/4 bar'; the theme, a dense middle, the theme again. Valse Hot: 'understating the third beat: instead of playing boom-tcheek-tcheek ... he plays boom-tcheek-(hush)'.

title: Alex Morris, Extended improvisations in the drumming of Max Roach and Kofi Ghanaba: rhythmic correspondences (MA thesis, Rutgers University-Newark, 2021)
notes: Abstract only read: transcription and analysis place Kofi Ghanaba's influence on Roach in 'complex ostinatos in long-form individual improvisations'. Met in Chicago in the mid 1950s; Roach visited him in Ghana in 1974.

title: Borut Rampih, Integration and development of jazz drum soloing (Research Catalogue)
notes: Transcribes Roach's solos on Mama (Percussion Bitter Sweet, 1961), Daahoud (1954) and Drum Conversation: question and answer at one-, two- and four-bar levels; 'Blazing fast triplets played around the set'; an 'ostinato hi-hat pattern' in Drum Conversation under the solo.

title: Diego Maldonado, Learning to solo in the style of Max Roach (Learn Jazz Standards, 18 October 2017)
notes: Parisian Thoroughfare (Clifford Brown & Max Roach, 1954): eighths and triplets in the A sections, sixteenths in the B; a motif from bar 3 brought back 'in the second A section and displaced it in a very interesting way'; 'a little triple idea which starts on the upbeats'.

title: Ted Panken, The Dozens: Nasheet Waits selects 12 classic Max Roach tracks (jazz.com)
notes: For Big Sid: theme and variation, call and response. Un Poco Loco (1951): 'its in phrases of 5 over the 4'. Garvey's Ghost: 'Max is kind of playing in 6 but also in 3'. Love Is a Many Splendored Thing (Basin Street, 1956) in 5/4. Triptych references 'that Drum Also Waltzes motif'. Din-Ka Street: no hi-hat on 2 and 4.

title: Fred Kaplan, Why Max Roach was jazz's greatest drummer (Slate, 22 August 2007)
notes: Un Poco Loco: 'a more complex layer that goes against Powell's rhythm, on a cowbell no less, while pounding a rumbling roll on the bass drum at a different tempo still'. 'Melody and tone clusters came as naturally to him as rhythm.'

title: Steve Boudreau, Bud Powell: Un Poco Loco
notes: The cowbell figure: 'a 5 over 4 pattern', 'slightly lopsided, not quite adding up to two bars'; it feels as if aimed at 'whole note triplets across the barline (this was hard to notate.)'. On the master take only. Two notations offered; neither settled.

title: Max Roach drum clinic and masterclass, Macalester College, 21 February 1991 (Practicing Drummer)
notes: On Ghanaian drumming: 'this hand will play two beats and this hand will play three beats'; 'if you want to play that instrument you have to learn how to play two against three'; independence as an attitude. About African percussion he studied, not a figure on a record of his.

title: Scott K. Fish, Max Roach: the quarter note is the common denominator (interview, 15 July 1981; Modern Drummer)
notes: 'the quarter note is the basic thing, regardless of the meter. It's like the common denominator.' All four limbs in quarters, balanced, as a practice drone. In the same Modern Drummer interview (via Todd Bishop, Max on the bass drum): in bebop the bass drum 'would only be used for accents and supports'.

title: Todd Bishop, Max on the bass drum (Cruise Ship Drummer, 16 May 2022)
notes: Quotes the 1981 Modern Drummer interview: the bass drum 'would only be used for accents and supports'; the 18-inch bass drum for travel. Bishop notes Roach in fact feathered the bass drum, which the interview leaves out.

title: Todd Bishop, Transcription: Blue Seven (Cruise Ship Drummer, 7 July 2012)
notes: Roach's solo on Blue 7 (Saxophone Colossus, 1956): starts four bars into a chorus, then six more twelve-bar choruses; 'maintaining quarter notes on the bass drum, lightly, and the 2 and 4 on the hihat all the way through'; the cymbal keeps the ride rhythm 'except to make an accent or set up the next thing'; paradiddle and double paradiddle stickings in the middle. Text read; the PDF's notes were not.

title: Todd Bishop, Transcription: Max comping (A Little Sweet; Cruise Ship Drummer, 2 May 2023)
notes: A Little Sweet (The Many Sides of Max), behind George Coleman, Booker Little and Julian Priester, 'tempo is about 230'. 'The cymbal rhythm is mostly consistent, and he plays the bass drum all the way through, pretty loudly', leaning on 4; 'a New Orleans kind of thing between the snare drum and bass drum'; an '& of 3 will be followed by an & of 2, and vice versa'; 'longer ideas, where he's phrasing in 3/4 within the 4/4 of the tune'; the hi-hat not loud on the record.

title: Todd Bishop, Transcription: Max soloing (A Little Sweet; Cruise Ship Drummer, 7 May 2023)
notes: His solo on A Little Sweet: 'Max's rubadub', 'a kind of rolling, integrated, New Orleans type of thing' between bass drum, cymbal and snare.

title: Todd Bishop, Transcription: Max fours (Minor Meeting; Cruise Ship Drummer, 10 May 2023)
notes: Minor Meeting (Sonny Clark Trio, Time, 1960): 'the tempo is a bright quarter note = 262'; 'Max plays the whole thing on snare drum, bass drum, and cymbals'; 'The beginning of most of these breaks is phrased in 3/4 time within 4/4'; 'On line 3 he plays a 4/4 idea twice, then displaces it'; line 6 'with a simple running 3/8 pattern'; 'a lot of six stroke rolls'.

title: Todd Bishop, Transcription: Max Roach comping (Flossie Lou; Cruise Ship Drummer, 18 March 2020)
notes: Behind Clifford Brown's 32 bars on Flossie Lou (At Basin Street sessions, 1956; a bonus track on the 2002 CD): the hi-hat on 2 and 4 throughout; bass drum throughout, accents written; 'Max always hits the cymbal on the downbeat after an accent on the & of 4'; a 'rubadub-like meter-within-meter phrase in the last four bars'.

title: Todd Bishop, How to play Jordu (Cruise Ship Drummer, 13 October 2013)
notes: Clifford Brown & Max Roach (EmArcy): AABA, 32 bars, figures and stops in the A sections; Roach plays the figure 'off the beat the first time, on the beat the second time, and off the beat again on the third time'; on the bridge 'a little set-up on the floor tom'; 'crescendoing 16th notes on the floor tom' on the second ending and before the solos.

title: Todd Bishop, Transcription: Max Roach - Garvey's Ghost (Cruise Ship Drummer, April 2011)
notes: A solo over an Afro-Cuban vamp (Percussion Bitter Sweet, 1961); 'Roach plays a jazz waltz behind the 6/4 Afro feel'. No ratio named; the PDF was not read.

title: Todd Bishop, Max's rubadub: transcribed phrases and cells (Cruise Ship Drummer, July-August 2019)
notes: Sonny Rollins's Freedom Suite, first section: 'a RLRR RLRR sticking pattern, in swing 8th notes; there are a lot of snare hits on the & of 1/3'; little audible hat foot. Max 'maintains the complete cymbal rhythm, which stays in 4 ... it doesn't have the running 3/4 feeling of Mel's thing'. The cells post: the three-beat cells 'you can also play in 4/4' and they resolve after three bars, which is Bishop's exercise, not a claim about the record.

title: Todd Bishop, Practice loop: Max in 5 (Cruise Ship Drummer, 10 January 2017)
notes: As Long As You're Living (Quiet As It's Kept): a twelve-bar blues in 5/4, 'quarter note = 186'. The groove is not described in the text.

title: AllSolos: Max Roach drums solo on Valse Hot
notes: Sonny Rollins Plus 4 (1956): 3/4, 141 bpm, a 16-bar form, two choruses of drum solo. Other AllSolos pages for him: St. Thomas 214, Daahoud 250, Joy Spring 166, Delilah 149, Moritat 165, Cherokee 360.

title: Weimar Jazz Database (Jazzomat Research Project): database content
notes: Measured tempos of the horn solos: Ko-Ko (Parker, 1945) 299.4; Jordu (1954) 139.0; Daahoud 240.9; Joy Spring 161.0; Blue Seven (1956) 134.6, 137.6, 133.3; St. Thomas 207.0, 224.1; I'll Remember April (1956) 285.4-294.0.

title: The Drum Also Waltzes - Max Roach - full drum transcription (Drumeo, via drumsetsheetmusic.com)
notes: Product page only: Drums Unlimited, 1966; tempo listed as 81 bpm, the note value not given; the time signature field garbled (a spreadsheet date where 3/4 was). The transcription itself was not read.

title: Ko-Ko - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded 26 November 1945, WOR studios, New York; Savoy 597. Parker, Gillespie (piano and trumpet), Curley Russell, Max Roach. A '32-bar drum solo from drummer Max Roach'; the drums 'tuned higher than normal'; he 'pushes forward the tempo'; about 300 bpm.

title: Clifford Brown & Max Roach - Wikipedia
notes: Capitol Studios, Hollywood, 2-6 August 1954 and 24-25 February 1955; EmArcy. Clifford Brown, Harold Land, Richie Powell, George Morrow, Max Roach. Daahoud, Joy Spring, Jordu, Parisian Thoroughfare, Delilah.

title: Clifford Brown and Max Roach at Basin Street - Wikipedia
notes: January and February 1956; Brown, Sonny Rollins, Richie Powell, George Morrow, Roach. Flossie Lou (Dameron) is a bonus track on the 2002 CD.

title: Sonny Rollins Plus 4 - Wikipedia
notes: Van Gelder Studio, 22 March 1956; Prestige, August 1956. Rollins, Clifford Brown, Richie Powell, George Morrow, Max Roach. Valse Hot and Pent-Up House (Rollins).

title: Saxophone Colossus - Wikipedia
notes: Van Gelder Studio, 22 June 1956; Prestige, 1957. Rollins, Tommy Flanagan, Doug Watkins, Max Roach. St. Thomas, You Don't Know What Love Is, Strode Rode, Moritat, Blue 7.

title: Jazz in 3/4 Time - Wikipedia
notes: September 1956 (track 7) and March 1957, Capitol Tower, Hollywood; EmArcy MG 36108, 1957. Roach, Kenny Dorham, Sonny Rollins, Billy Wallace or Ray Bryant, George Morrow. Blues Waltz and Little Folks (Roach), Valse Hot (Rollins), I'll Take Romance, Lover, The Most Beautiful Girl in the World. Six songs in waltz time.

title: Sonny Clark Trio (Time T 70010, 1960): Fresh Sound Records catalogue entry and The 1960 Time Sessions reissue
notes: Read through search results (the catalogue, the 2017 Tompkins Square reissue, a library record), not the page itself. New York, 23 March 1960: Sonny Clark (piano), George Duvivier (bass), Max Roach (drums). Minor Meeting, Nica, Sonny's Crip, Blues Mambo, Blues Blue, Junka, My Conception, Sonia.

title: The Many Sides of Max - Wikipedia
notes: Fine Recording, New York, 22 January 1959; Mercury MG 20911, 1964. Roach, Booker Little, Julian Priester, George Coleman, Art Davis. A Little Sweet and Tympanalli (Roach).

title: Drums Unlimited - Wikipedia
notes: Atlantic Studios, 14 and 20 October 1965 and 25 April 1966; Atlantic 1467, 1966. The Drum Also Waltzes (Roach, 3:34, 14 October 1965), the title track and For Big Sid are unaccompanied; Freddie Hubbard, James Spaulding, Ronnie Mathews and Jymie Merritt on the others.

title: We Insist! - Wikipedia
notes: Nola Penthouse, New York, 31 August and 6 September 1960; Candid, January 1961. Abbey Lincoln; Babatunde Olatunji, Ray Mantilla and Tomas du Vall on percussion (side two). Driva' Man in 5/4 with a hit on every 1; the drums tuned to Lincoln's voice in Triptych.
